propositions.text: Whether union members formerly represented by their union have standing to maintain judicial review of an adjudicator's negative decision when the union no longer represents them but authorizes continuation.
propositions.quote: The principal issue raised on this consolidated application for judicial review is whether union members, formerly represented by their union at the grievance and adjudication phases, have standing to maintain an application for judicial review challenging a negative decision of an adjudicator in circumstances where the grievance relates to the interpretation of a provision of the collective agreement and their union no longer represents them, but purports to authorize the continuation of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the main issue is whether former union members have standing to pursue judicial review when their union no longer represents them but authorizes continuation.

propositions.text: The standing issue arises in the following factual context.
propositions.quote: This issue arises in the following factual context.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the standing issue arises in the following factual context.

propositions.text: Applicants were employed as large-file appeals officers at the AU-04 level at Canada Revenue Agency in Calgary and were union members under a collective agreement.
propositions.quote: At all material times, the applicants were employed by the Canada Revenue Agency as large-file appeals officers at the AU-04 level in the Tax Services Office in Calgary, Alberta. The applicants were all members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada and a collective agreement existed between the Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants were employed at CRA as AU-04 officers and were union members under a collective agreement.

propositions.text: Applicants filed grievances alleging employer violated clause 45.07 requiring acting pay for duties at higher classification for three consecutive days.
propositions.quote: The applicants, and others, filed grievances alleging that their employer had violated clause 45.07 of the collective agreement. This clause requires the payment of acting pay to an employee when the employee is required by the employer to substantially perform the duties of a higher classification level on an acting basis for three consecutive working days.

propositions.text: Applicants alleged they performed duties of AU-05 and AU-06 positions for a lengthy period.
propositions.quote: The applicants alleged that for a lengthy period they had been performing the duties associated with the positions classified at the AU-05 and AU-06 group and levels.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants filed grievances alleging violation of acting pay clause and performing higher-level duties for a lengthy period.

propositions.text: Grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication under subsection 209(1) of FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: The grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication pursuant to subsection 209(1) of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, s. 2 (FPSLR Act or Act).

propositions.text: Because grievance related to interpretation or application of collective agreement, applicants obtained Institute's approval to represent them in adjudication as required by subsection 209(2).
propositions.quote: Because the grievance related to “the interpretation or application in respect of the employee of a provision of a collective agreement”, the applicants obtained, as they were required to obtain, the approval of the Institute to represent them in the adjudication proceedings (subsection 209(2) of the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The court states grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication with Institute's approval as required by law.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found she lacked jurisdiction as issues were classification, not acting pay.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator found that she was without jurisdiction to consider the grievances because the issues raised were issues of classification — not issues of acting pay.

propositions.text: Adjudicator held that if incorrect, Institute failed to show grievors assigned work outside AU-04 job description.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator went on to hold that if she was incorrect in that finding, the Institute had failed to meet the burden of showing that the grievors were assigned work outside the scope of the job description for their AU-04 large-file appeals officer positions (2017 PSLREB 45).

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator found no jurisdiction as issues were classification, and alternatively Institute failed to prove grievors worked outside AU-04 scope.

propositions.text: Institute retained counsel to apply for judicial review; counsel filed applications for each applicant.
propositions.quote: The Institute retained counsel to commence an application for judicial review of the adjudicator’s decision, and counsel filed an application on behalf of each of the three applicants.

propositions.text: After discussions, applicants decided to represent themselves on judicial review and have done so since.
propositions.quote: After privileged discussions between the Institute and the applicants, it was decided that the applicants would represent themselves on the application for judicial review. Thereafter the applicants have represented themselves.

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator reports Institute retained counsel for judicial review but applicants chose to self-represent thereafter.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants lack standing to pursue judicial review.
propositions.quote: In response, the respondent Attorney General argues that the applicants lack standing to pursue their application.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent Attorney General argues applicants lack standing to pursue judicial review.

propositions.text: Institute granted intervenor status on standing issue; Institute's General Counsel swore Institute supports continuation of application.
propositions.quote: The Institute was granted intervenor status in the application on the issue of whether the applicants have standing to pursue the application for judicial review in circumstances where they are no longer represented by the Institute’s counsel. The Institute’s General Counsel and Chief of Labour Relations Services has filed an affidavit in which she swears that the “Institute continues to authorize, support and approve the continuation” of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute was intervenor and swore it supports continuation of the judicial review application.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review consolidated with others filed by applicants after procedural removal; reasons to be placed in each file.
propositions.quote: By order dated August 29, 2018, the application for judicial review was consolidated with other applications later filed by the applicants Mr. Fong and Mr. Leung after they were removed as parties from the original application for procedural reasons. A copy of these reasons shall be placed in each file.

paragraphs.summary: The court ordered consolidation of judicial review applications and placement of reasons in each file.

propositions.text: Issues: standing to pursue judicial review; adjudicator's jurisdiction; procedural fairness or bias; reliance on perjured evidence.
propositions.quote: I would frame the issues raised by the applicants on this consolidated application to be: Do the applicants have standing to pursue the application for judicial review? Did the adjudicator commit a reviewable error in finding that she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate on the grievances? Did the adjudicator breach the applicants’ rights to procedural fairness or act in a manner that gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias? Did the adjudicator rely upon perjured evidence?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames issues as standing, adjudicator's jurisdiction, procedural fairness or bias, and reliance on perjured evidence.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants lack standing as not directly affected persons under Federal Courts Act; only union can pursue grievance under exclusivity principle.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the Attorney General argues that the applicants are not persons directly affected by the decision of the adjudicator as required by subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, because they seek a benefit under the collective agreement. However, they are not parties to this contract which is exclusively between the Institute and the Canada Revenue Agency. Counsel further argues that exclusivity between an employer and a union is a key principle in labour relations, and under this principle only the union can pursue a grievance.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues applicants lack standing as only the union can pursue grievances under exclusivity principle.

propositions.text: Applicant Insch argues he has statutory and common law standing; signed grievance; Institute supports application; directly affected by denial of acting pay and alleged misconduct.
propositions.quote: The applicant Ken Insch argues that he has both statutory and common law standing because the FPSLR Act contemplates judicial review in subsection 209(2), he signed the grievance and the Institute supports this application. He further argues that he is directly affected by the adjudicator’s decision that denied him acting pay. Further, he argues he is directly affected by the fraud, perjury and egregious conduct that took place before the adjudicator and that the “government” owed him a duty of fairness. The other applicants adopt these submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant Insch argues he has standing, signed grievance, Institute supports, and he is directly affected by denial and alleged misconduct.

propositions.text: Institute acknowledges it must support judicial review applications on collective agreement interpretation; only union has carriage of disputes before Board to ensure unified representation.
propositions.quote: The Institute responds to the submissions of the Attorney General by acknowledging that the Institute must support any judicial review application relating to the interpretation or administration of the collective agreement. Citing cases such as Noël v. Société d'énergie de la Baie James, 2001 SCC 39, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 207 at paragraph 62 and Migneault v. New Brunswick (Board of Management), 2016 NBCA 52, 452 N.B.R. (2d) 223, the Institute submits that it is the union alone that has carriage of disputes before the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (Board) that concern the interpretation and application of the governing collective agreement. This requirement ensures that individual union members cannot advance an argument about the interpretation or application of a collective agreement that is not supported by the union as representative of all of the members of the relevant bargaining unit.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits only the union has carriage of disputes before the Board to ensure unified representation.

propositions.text: Under FPSLR Act, individual grievor files grievance and becomes applicant or respondent in judicial review, differing from other jurisdictions.
propositions.quote: This said, the Institute submits that the grievance and adjudication scheme under the FPSLR Act and its predecessor is structured differently than in most other jurisdictions: under the Act it is the individual grievor who files the grievance in their name. Under this scheme it is the grievor who then becomes the applicant or respondent in an application for judicial review of a decision of an adjudicator.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits FPSLR Act scheme differs as individual grievor files grievance and becomes applicant in judicial review.

propositions.text: Institute must continue to support judicial review applications to maintain autonomy in policing collective agreement.
propositions.quote: The Institute submits, however, that it must continue to support any judicial review application relating to the interpretation or administration of the collective agreement, as it has in this case. Otherwise, its autonomy in policing the collective agreement would be undermined.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits it must support judicial review applications to maintain autonomy in policing the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Before considering standing, court will refer to relevant provisions of collective agreement and FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: Before beginning consideration of this issue it is helpful to first refer to the relevant provisions of the collective agreement and the FPSLR Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court will first refer to relevant provisions of the collective agreement and FPSLR Act before considering standing.

propositions.text: The collective agreement is between Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.
propositions.quote: The collective agreement is between the Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the collective agreement is between Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

propositions.text: Article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees covered by certificate issued December 12, 2001, including applicants.
propositions.quote: In article 25 of the collective agreement the employer recognized “the Institute as the exclusive bargaining agent for all employees described in the certificate issued by the Public Service Staff Relations Board on December 12, 2001, covering employees of the Audit, Financial and Scientific bargaining unit currently classified in accordance with” specified classification standards. The applicants were employees described in this certificate.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees including applicants.

propositions.text: No provision grants individual employee unfettered right to pursue grievance if it relates to interpretation or application of collective agreement.
propositions.quote: No provision of the collective agreement grants to an individual employee the unfettered right to pursue a grievance at any level if the grievance relates to the interpretation or application of a provision of the collective agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no provision grants individual employee unfettered right to pursue grievance on collective agreement interpretation or application.

propositions.text: Article 34 of the agreement limits grievance procedure rights, requiring union approval and representation for individual grievances.
propositions.quote: An important limitation is found in article 34.07, which prevents an employee from presenting “an individual grievance relating to the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement … unless the employee has the approval of and is represented by the Institute.”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds article 34.07 limits grievance rights, requiring union approval and representation for individual grievances.

propositions.text: Article 34.22 similarly requires union approval before an individual grievance can be referred to adjudication.
propositions.quote: Similarly, article 34.22 precludes an employee from referring to adjudication an individual grievance relating to “the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement” without the approval of the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds article 34.22 requires union approval before referring individual grievances to adjudication.

propositions.text: Article 34 provisions largely reflect legislated requirements under the FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: It will be seen from the following review of the relevant provisions of the FPSLR Act that the provisions of article 34 of the collective agreement in large measure reflect legislated requirements.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds article 34 provisions largely reflect legislated requirements under the FPSLR Act.

propositions.text: The FPSLR Act preamble emphasizes mutual respect and harmonious labour-management relations as essential to effective public service.
propositions.quote: The preamble to the Act recognizes that a “commitment from the employer and bargaining agents to mutual respect and harmonious labour-management relations is essential to a productive and effective public service”.

propositions.text: The preamble recognizes bargaining agents represent employees in collective bargaining and workplace dispute resolution.
propositions.quote: The preamble also recognizes that “public service bargaining agents represent the interests of employees in collective bargaining and participate in the resolution of workplace issues and rights disputes”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the FPSLR Act preamble emphasizes mutual respect and bargaining agents' role in employee representation and dispute resolution.

propositions.text: Subsection 2(1) defines a collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent about employment terms.
propositions.quote: Subsection 2(1) defines a “collective agreement” to be an agreement in writing “between the employer and a bargaining agent, containing provisions respecting terms and conditions of employment and related matters.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 2(1) defines a collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent.

propositions.text: Part 1 of the Act defines parties as employer and bargaining agent for collective bargaining and disputes; Part 2 has no parties definition.
propositions.quote: Part 1 of the Act, dealing with “Labour Relations”, defines “parties”, in relation to collective bargaining, arbitration, conciliation or a dispute, to mean “the employer and the bargaining agent.” (subsection 4(1)). Part 2 of the Act, dealing with “Grievances”, contains no definition of “parties”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Part 1 defines parties as employer and bargaining agent; Part 2 has no parties definition.

propositions.text: Subsection 208(1) entitles employees to present individual grievances about collective agreement interpretation or application.
propositions.quote: Subsection 208(1) of the Act states that “an employee is entitled to present an individual grievance” if the employee feels aggrieved “by the interpretation or application … of … a provision of a collective agreement”.

propositions.text: Subsection 208(4) requires employee to have bargaining agent's approval and representation to present grievance.
propositions.quote: The employee may only present the grievance if the employee “has the approval of and is represented by the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit to which the collective agreement” applies (subsection 208(4)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 208(1) entitles employees to present grievances with bargaining agent approval and representation required by subsection 208(4).

propositions.text: Subsection 209(1) permits employees to refer individual grievances to adjudication about collective agreement interpretation or application.
propositions.quote: Subsection 209(1) similarly permits an employee to refer to adjudication an individual grievance relating to “the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement”.

propositions.text: Subsection 209(2) requires employee to obtain bargaining agent's approval to represent them in adjudication.
propositions.quote: Prior to referring the grievance, the employee must obtain “the approval of his or her bargaining agent to represent him or her in the adjudication proceedings.” (subsection 209(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 209(1) permits grievance referral to adjudication with bargaining agent approval required by subsection 209(2).

propositions.text: Regulations require employee presenting individual grievance to provide declaration of bargaining agent's approval and representation.
propositions.quote: Section 67 of the Regulations permits an employee to present an individual grievance, while subsection 69(1) requires that a grievor who presents an individual grievance relating to the interpretation or application of a collective agreement must provide a declaration from the authorized representative of the appropriate bargaining agent indicating that the grievor, in presenting the grievance, has the approval of and is represented by the bargaining agent.

propositions.text: Notice of reference to adjudication must be filed in Form 20 with bargaining agent's declaration of willingness to represent.
propositions.quote: Subsection 89(1) of the Regulations provides that a notice of reference to adjudication for individual grievances relating to the interpretation or application of a provision of the collective agreement shall be filed in Form 20 of the schedule. Form 20 collects information about the grievor and concludes with a declaration, in accordance with subsection 89(3), by an authorized representative of the applicable bargaining agent indicating that the bargaining agent is willing to represent the grievor in the adjudication proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states regulations require declarations of bargaining agent approval and representation for grievances and adjudication notices.

propositions.text: Adjudication rights arise from legislation, not the collective agreement, entitling employees to present grievances and refer to adjudication.
propositions.quote: The above review of the relevant provisions of the Act, Regulations and the collective agreement shows that adjudication rights in the federal public sector arise directly from the legislation and not the collective agreement: subject to the limitations described above, subsection 208(1) of the Act entitles an employee to present an individual grievance and subsection 209(1) entitles employees such as the applicants to refer individual grievances to adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adjudication rights arise from legislation, not the collective agreement, entitling employees to present grievances and refer to adjudication.

propositions.text: Parties to adjudication are individual grievors and employer; union approves and represents but is not a party.
propositions.quote: Consistent with this legislation, the parties to an adjudication of an individual grievance before the Board are the individual grievors and the employer. The union is not a party but instead approves of and represents the employee at the grievance and adjudication stages.

propositions.text: Applicants are not exercising adjudication rights under the collective agreement between the Institute and the Canada Revenue Agency.
propositions.quote: Therefore, contrary to the submissions of the Attorney General, the applicants are not exercising adjudication rights under the collective agreement between the Institute and the Canada Revenue Agency.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties to adjudication are grievors and employer; union represents but is not party; applicants not exercising rights under collective agreement.

propositions.text: Legislative scheme ousts contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General for adjudication rights.
propositions.quote: This legislative scheme, at least in respect of adjudication rights for individual grievances, ousts the requirement of contractual privity relied on by the Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the legislative scheme ousts contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General.

propositions.text: Federal Courts Act s.18.1(1) permits anyone directly affected to apply for judicial review.
propositions.quote: Subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act permits anyone “directly affected by the matter in respect of which relief is sought” to apply for judicial review.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants are not directly affected and lack standing to seek judicial review.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General has not demonstrated how as parties to an adjudication brought by the applicants under this statutory scheme, the applicants are not “directly affected” by the decision they seek to review.

propositions.text: Applicants have standing to commence and pursue judicial review as parties directly affected by adjudicator's decision.
propositions.quote: As parties to the adjudicator’s decision, the applicants have standing to commence and pursue this application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Federal Courts Act allows judicial review by those directly affected; Attorney General disputes applicants' standing; court finds applicants have standing.

propositions.text: The legislative scheme poses difficulty for the union's proper role at judicial review stage.
propositions.quote: This said, I acknowledge the difficulty posed by this legislative scheme to the proper role of a union at the judicial review stage.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges the legislative scheme poses difficulty for union's role at judicial review stage.

propositions.text: Board and predecessors hold grievor may only proceed if represented by bargaining agent for grievances on collective agreement interpretation or application.
propositions.quote: The Board and its predecessors have consistently held that when a grievance relates to the interpretation or application of a collective agreement the grievor may only proceed if represented by his or her bargaining agent (see, for example, Cavanagh v. Canada Revenue Agency, 2014 PSLRB 21, [2014] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 21; Boivin v. Treasury Board (Canada Border Services Agency), 2009 PSLRB 98, [2009] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 98).

propositions.text: If bargaining agent withdraws support, grievance is no longer adjudicable.
propositions.quote: In such cases, if a bargaining agent subsequently withdraws its support, the grievance is no longer adjudicable (Yarney v. Deputy Head (Department of Health), 2011 PSLRB 112, [2011] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 111).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found grievors need bargaining agent representation for grievances; withdrawal of support ends adjudicability.

propositions.text: No similar statutory requirement exists for union representation at judicial review of adjudicator's negative decision.
propositions.quote: However, as the above review of the legislative regime and the collective agreement demonstrates, no similar statutory requirement exists when an employee pursues an application for judicial review of a negative decision of an adjudicator.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no statutory requirement for union representation at judicial review of adjudicator's negative decision.

propositions.text: At grievance and adjudication stages, union representation protects all members' rights in collective agreement interpretation or application.
propositions.quote: At the grievance and adjudication stages the rights of all of the union’s members are protected by the requirement that the union represent grievors.

propositions.text: It makes little sense to lose union representation protection at judicial review, which has greater precedential value.
propositions.quote: In my view it makes little sense for the protection provided by union representation at the grievance and adjudication stages to be surrendered on judicial review — a proceeding that carries greater precedential value than grievance or adjudication proceedings.

propositions.text: Legislation provides no solution when union member pursues judicial review but union does not.
propositions.quote: However, the legislation provides no solution for the relatively rare situations when a union member wishes to pursue judicial review but the union does not.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds union representation protects members at grievance and adjudication; losing it at judicial review is illogical; legislation offers no solution if union declines review.

propositions.text: Institute submits union retains ultimate grievance control as it will represent grievors if matter remitted to adjudication.
propositions.quote: The Institute submits that in this circumstance the union maintains ultimate control of the grievance because if this Court remits the matter back to adjudication, the union will represent the grievors at adjudication.

propositions.text: This submission overlooks court's power to issue binding directions or direct outcome on judicial review.
propositions.quote: This, however, overlooks the potential for this Court to issue binding directions to an adjudicator or, in an exceptional case, to direct the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits union retains control if matter remitted; court finds this overlooks its power to issue binding directions or outcomes.

propositions.text: Institute counsel drafted judicial review notice, but applicants argue issues not raised by counsel, including inadequate representation and perjury allegations.
propositions.quote: Further, in the present case while counsel for the Institute did draft the notice of application seeking judicial review, in the consolidated application the applicants argue issues not raised by counsel in the application: that the applicants were inadequately represented by the Institute and that the employer, through specifically named employees, presented perjured evidence.

propositions.text: Serious unfiltered perjury allegations against co-workers may harm harmonious labour-management relations, a consequence of absent union representation on judicial review.
propositions.quote: Such a serious, unfiltered allegation of perjury made against co-workers cannot promote harmonious labour-management relations. Yet, it is a consequence that may flow from the absence of union representation on judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicants raise new issues including perjury allegations, which may harm labour relations without union representation on judicial review.

propositions.text: There may be a way to respect union's responsibility to protect bargaining unit interests on judicial review when collective agreement issues arise.
propositions.quote: There is, perhaps, one way to recognize and respect on judicial review a union’s responsibility to ensure that the interests of the bargaining unit as a whole are protected when issues concerning the application or interpretation of a collective agreement are raised.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue of a possible way to respect union's responsibility to protect bargaining unit interests on judicial review.

propositions.text: Rule 303(1) requires naming as respondent every person directly affected by the order sought, except the tribunal.
propositions.quote: Rule 303(1) of the Federal Courts Rules, in subpart (a), requires an applicant to name as a respondent every person “directly affected by the order sought in the application, other than a tribunal in respect of which the application is brought”

propositions.text: Applicants no longer represented by their union may be required to name the union as respondent and serve notice on it.
propositions.quote: It may be that applicants who are no longer represented by their union on judicial review are required by this Rule to name the union as respondent in their notice of application and to serve their notice of application upon the union.

propositions.text: Compliance with Rule 303(1) ensures affected union receives notice and can participate to protect bargaining unit interests.
propositions.quote: Compliance with Rule 303(1) would ensure that an affected union receives notice of such an application and would permit the union to choose to participate in the proceeding to ensure that in matters that implicate the interpretation or application of the collective agreement the interests of the bargaining unit as a whole are represented and protected.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 303(1) requires naming affected persons as respondents, possibly including unions, to ensure notice and participation.

propositions.text: Whether the adjudicator erred in finding she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the grievances.
propositions.quote: Did the adjudicator commit a reviewable error in finding that she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate on the grievances?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether the adjudicator erred in finding lack of jurisdiction over grievances.

propositions.text: The standard of review for the adjudicator's jurisdiction finding should be correctness.
propositions.quote: applicants’ submission that the standard of review of correctness should be applied to the adjudicator’s finding that she lacked jurisdiction to consider the grievances

propositions.text: The adjudicator's jurisdiction decision is reviewed for reasonableness, not correctness, citing precedents.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator’s decision that she lacked jurisdiction is properly reviewed for reasonableness: Nadeau v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 203, [2018] F.C.J. No. 1133, paragraph 16; Klos v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 160, [2018] F.C.J. No. 916, paragraphs 1-3.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue for correctness standard; court finds reasonableness standard applies to adjudicator's jurisdiction decision.

propositions.text: Adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances as classification issues, constituting abuse of discretion and jurisdiction error.
propositions.quote: applicants’ submission that by misconstruing the grievances to raise an issue of classification the adjudicator committed an error of law that rose to the level of an abuse of discretion and an error of jurisdiction

propositions.text: There is no merit to the applicants' submission that the adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances as classification issues.
propositions.quote: There is equally no merit to the applicants’ submission that by misconstruing the grievances to raise an issue of classification the adjudicator committed an error of law that rose to the level of an abuse of discretion and an error of jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances; court finds no merit in this submission.

propositions.text: Applicants made few submissions addressing adjudicator's jurisdiction finding and do not point to clear errors in reasoning.
propositions.quote: The applicants made few if any submissions directly addressing the adjudicator’s finding that she lacked jurisdiction; the applicants do not point to any clear errors in the adjudicator’s reasoning.

propositions.text: Applicants mainly argue their case anew and on fraudulent concealment, which the Board did not decide due to lack of jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Rather, the bulk of the applicants’ submissions focus on arguing their case de novo and on the issue of fraudulent concealment, a matter not determined by the Board in view of its finding that it lacked jurisdiction.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicants did not address jurisdiction finding errors but argued case anew and on fraudulent concealment not decided by Board.

propositions.text: Adjudicator referred to Bungay decision describing characteristics distinguishing classification from acting pay grievances.
propositions.quote: the adjudicator referred to the decision of Bungay v. Treasury Board (Department of Public Works and Government Services), 2005 PSLRB 40, [2005] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 42, where, at paragraph 59, the Board provided a non-exhaustive description of the characteristics that distinguish a classification grievance from an acting pay grievance.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes adjudicator referred to Bungay decision describing classification versus acting pay grievances.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns related to entire duties since appointment and consistent over time, suggesting chronic undervaluation.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator found that the applicants’ concerns related to the entirety of their duties since their respective appointments to the AU-04 large-file appeals officer positions and that their duties had been consistent over time. This suggested that the applicants’ concern was that their work had been chronically undervalued.

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns related to entire duties and consistent work, suggesting chronic undervaluation.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found grievances related to classification based on evidence and comparison with counterparts.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator further considered that the applicants’ grievances were in part based on a comparison with the work of their counterparts in another appeals office. The adjudicator then looked at the essence of the applicants’ complaint and found that the issues they raised related to classification (reasons, paragraph 224).

propositions.text: This factual determination is entitled to deference and was not shown to be unreasonable by applicants.
propositions.quote: This was a heavily factually-suffused determination, based on the adjudicator’s appreciation of the evidence. It is a determination that is entitled to deference. The applicants have not demonstrated that the finding was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found grievances related to classification; court defers and finds no unreasonableness shown.

propositions.text: Adjudicator breached procedural fairness by excluding some evidence and allowing all employer evidence, causing bias.
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the adjudicator breached their right to procedural fairness by failing to admit some of their evidence, while allowing all of their employer’s evidence. This is said to have resulted in a biased procedure.

propositions.text: Adjudicator showed reasonable apprehension of bias by relying almost exclusively on employer testimony despite equal credibility of applicants.
propositions.quote: The applicants further submit that the adjudicator demonstrated a reasonable apprehension of bias since she used the employer’s “representatives’ testimony almost exclusively as the basis for the Decision even though the Applicants were found to be equally credible.”

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege procedural fairness breach and reasonable apprehension of bias due to evidence exclusion and reliance on employer testimony.

propositions.text: Applicants argue evidence was excluded as outside grievance period.
propositions.quote: The applicants argue that their evidence was excluded on the basis that it was from “outside the grievance period.”

propositions.text: No transcript exists; court relies on affidavit evidence to assess evidence exclusion.
propositions.quote: There is no transcript of the hearing before the adjudicator, which makes this Court reliant on affidavit evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue evidence excluded as outside grievance period; court notes reliance on affidavit evidence due to no transcript.

propositions.text: Adjudicator excluded June 2, 2005 memorandum because sender/contact did not testify and document related to different division.
propositions.quote: with respect to a memorandum dated June 2, 2005 – relating to ratings for files in the Audit Division – the affidavit of a representative of the employer is to the effect that neither the sender nor the contact person indicated on the document testified and the bargaining agent did not call any witness who had received the document. Further, the document only spoke about the Audit Division; the applicants were employed in the Appeals Division.

propositions.text: These facts justified exclusion of the memorandum; employer's representative was not challenged in cross-examination.
propositions.quote: These facts would justify exclusion of the memorandum and the employer’s representative was not challenged in cross-examination on her evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds exclusion of June 2, 2005 memorandum justified due to lack of testimony and division relevance.

propositions.text: March 21, 2003 memorandum excluded because no witness connected it to applicant and no sender/recipient testified.
propositions.quote: the document was excluded because the bargaining agent could not connect it to the witness, the applicant Mr. Fong. Neither the sender nor the recipient of the memorandum or the purported author testified at the hearing.

propositions.text: These facts justified exclusion of the memorandum.
propositions.quote: These facts would also justify exclusion of this memorandum.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds exclusion of March 21, 2003 memorandum justified due to lack of witness connection and testimony.

propositions.text: Similar examples of evidence exclusion exist.
propositions.quote: Similar examples exist.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes other similar examples of evidence exclusion exist.

propositions.text: Courts should not substitute their view of evidence relevance except when exclusion breaches natural justice.
propositions.quote: Courts generally should not substitute their view of the relevance of evidence for that of the decision-maker except when the rejection of relevant evidence has such an impact on the fairness of the proceeding that it unavoidably leads to the conclusion that there is been a breach of natural justice (Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières v. Larocque, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 471, at page 491).

propositions.text: Adjudicator dismissed evidence for reasons beyond grievance period, not solely on that basis.
propositions.quote: while the applicants suggest that the adjudicator dismissed evidence on the basis that it was from outside the grievance period, the adjudicator appears to have dismissed the evidence for other reasons as well.

paragraphs.summary: Court states courts defer to decision-maker on evidence relevance unless natural justice breached; adjudicator dismissed evidence for multiple reasons.

propositions.text: No basis to find documents were improperly excluded causing breach of natural justice or bias without better evidence from applicants.
propositions.quote: In the absence of better evidence from the applicants I see no basis to find that documents were improperly excluded in a fashion that demonstrates any breach of natural justice or any reasonable apprehension of bias.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no basis to conclude improper evidence exclusion breached natural justice or caused bias without better evidence.

propositions.text: Adjudicator's reliance on employer evidence does not support bias allegation.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the adjudicator’s reliance upon evidence adduced by representatives of the employer cannot support the applicants’ allegation of bias.

propositions.text: Bias is serious and requires evidence showing reasonable apprehension of unfairness to a reasonable, informed person.
propositions.quote: Bias is a serious allegation. The applicants have not brought any evidence or argument that would demonstrate to a reasonable, fully informed person, thinking the matter through, that it is more likely than not that the adjudicator would not decide the matter before her fairly (Committee for Justice and Liberty v. Canada (National Energy Board), [1978] 1 S.C.R. 369, at page 394).

propositions.text: Disagreement with adjudicator's evidence assessment does not amount to valid bias claim.
propositions.quote: Mere disagreement with the way in which the adjudicator assessed conflicting evidence does not give rise to a valid claim of bias.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no bias from reliance on employer evidence; bias requires serious evidence and mere disagreement is insufficient.

propositions.text: Applicants allege Canada Revenue Agency submitted perjured evidence through employees.
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the Canada Revenue Agency, through its employees, submitted perjured evidence.

propositions.text: Perjury is serious and must be supported by more than mere assertion.
propositions.quote: Perjury is also a serious allegation that must be supported by more than mere assertion (Rafizadeh v. Toronto-Dominion Bank, 2014 FCA 144, 461 N.R. 318, paragraph 8).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege perjury by Canada Revenue Agency employees; court states perjury requires more than assertion.

propositions.text: Applicants argue every contradiction is continuation of fraud by management team.
propositions.quote: the applicants’ submissions are to the effect that since fraud has been perpetrated against them by their management team, every contradiction in the evidence is an apparent continuation of the fraud.

propositions.text: Alleged lies or perjury are disagreements with evidence and requests to reweigh evidence, not proven perjury.
propositions.quote: the alleged lies or instances of perjury are best characterized as disagreements with the evidence adduced on behalf of the Canada Revenue Agency, and many of the applicants’ submissions on this issue amount to a request to reweigh the evidence that was before the adjudicator. The applicants have fallen well short of demonstrating perjury.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants claim contradictions are fraud continuation; court finds these are disagreements, not proven perjury.

propositions.text: Dismiss application for judicial review; adjudicator's jurisdiction decision was reasonable and not tainted by bias or impropriety.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the application for judicial review on the basis that the decision of the adjudicator that the Board lacked jurisdiction was reasonable, and the applicants have failed to demonstrate that this conclusion was tainted by bias or other impropriety.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application, finding adjudicator's jurisdiction decision reasonable and unbiased.

propositions.text: No order as to costs due to divided success on issues before the Court.
propositions.quote: As success on the issues before the Court was divided I would not make any order as to costs.

paragraphs.summary: Court declines to order costs due to divided success on issues.
